1-2: Days of the week counted forward or back: tomorrow, the day before yesterday, or some days on or ago.
Ages some years on or some years ago, and the difference between two ages, which stays the same.
Weeks and days: the days in a few weeks.
Holidays from one day to another, both ends counted.
Dates across the end of a month: the days left until a birthday, or the date some days later.
A month's page: the day of the week of a date, from the day the 1st falls on.
Something done every few days: how many times it comes in a month.
The months in order: the month that comes some months after another, across the new year.
Two birthdays in one year: the child born earlier in the year is the older one.
School days and days off, as the task names them: how many of each there are in a few weeks.
A stay of some nights away: it takes one day more than nights, the day of leaving and the day of coming home both counted.
Two or three ages added together: each year the total grows by one year for every person.
3-4: Three of one day of the week falling on even dates in a month: dates a week apart change between even and odd, so there are five of that day, the first on the 2nd.
How many times as old a parent is as a child.
Days in a few months together.
A month whose days of the week come four or five times: those that come five times are its first days, as many as its days over four weeks, so they tell the day of the 1st.
Ages that seem to jump, such as ten the day before yesterday and thirteen next year: a birthday on the last day of the year, said on the first day of the next.
A birthday on 29 February: the birthdays on the real date in a run of years, with a leap year every fourth.
The first Tuesday of a month and its first Tuesday after the first Monday, or any such pair of days: the same day unless the month's first Tuesday comes before its first Monday.
Something done on odd dates only: where a month ends on an odd date, the 31st or a leap year's 29 February, it comes two days running at the turn.
Ages in a ratio that add up to a given total.
Dates next to each other or a week apart on a month's page: three of them in a row add up to three times the middle one, which finds them from their sum.
A trip from one day of the week to a later one whose date is smaller: a new month began on the way, so the two dates are tied by that month's length.
5-6: The day of the week of a date one or more years later, each leap day between adding a day.
The number of a day in a leap year or another, and the date that day falls on.
An age, from what it will be in some years and what it was some years ago.
The ages of two people at two moments, ten years apart.
The rule of leap years, the century years among them.
Three generations: ages that add up, and how old each was when the next was born.
A family's ages that add up now and some years ago, when one child was not yet born.
The next year in which a date falls on the same day of the week.
Something that happens every so many hours, such as every 50 hours: the day of the week and the hour it comes round.
Two things done every few days, such as every 4th and every 6th day: the next day they fall together.
Flowers that stay yellow for some days and then white for some more before they fade: counting each by the day it opened ties the counts of different days together.
Something that depends only on the day of the week, such as the price of a lunch: any seven days in a row cost the same, the price of one whole week.
A count that grows by the same amount every day, known on the 1st and on the last day of a month: the days between, one fewer than the month's, must divide the growth.
An age counted in whole months and in whole years: the months are twelve times the years plus those since the last birthday, so the two counts give the year and the month of birth.
An age equal to the last two digits of the year of birth, or to the sum of its digits: the year of birth is found from the year it is said in, one century at a time.
Days named through other days, such as 'when the day after tomorrow is yesterday': each phrase moves the day by a few, and the moves add up.
Two ages written with the same two digits the other way round: their difference is nine times the difference of the digits, and their sum eleven times the digits' sum.
Children born at equal gaps of years: the eldest is older than the youngest by one gap fewer than there are children, whatever their ages now.
The years in which a parent's age is a whole number of times a child's: they come when the child's age divides the difference of their ages, which never changes.
Ages told through each other's past, such as 'twice as old as you were when I was as old as you are now': the difference of the two ages never changes.
